L	My observations of No. 427, Park Lane did little to resolve the problem that occupied my mind.
The house, separated from the street by a low wall and railing, was easily accessible from the
garden, yet the window itself remained beyond reach. There was no pipe, no ledge—nothing to
assist even the most agile intruder. Still perplexed, I returned to my study in Kensington, my
thoughts unsettled by the contradiction.
Thad scarcely settled in when the maid entered.
“A person desires to see you, sir,” she said.
“Who is it?” I asked.
Before she could respond, the visitor appeared. To my astonishment, it was the same elderly
book collector I had encountered earlier—his sharp, wizened face framed in white hair, his
arms burdened with volumes.
“You're surprised to see me, sir,” he said in a strange, croaking voice.
“T confess that I am,” I replied.
“Well, I’ve a conscience, sir,” he continued. “When I saw you enter this house, I thought I
would step in and assure you that if I seemed gruff earlier, no offense was intended. I am much
obliged to you for picking up my books.”
“You make too much of a trifle,” I said. “But tell me—how did you know who I was?”
“Tf it isn’t too great a liberty,” he answered, “I am your neighbour. My bookshop stands at the
corner of Church Street. You may visit any time. Perhaps you are a collector yourself? I have
British Birds, Catullus, and The Holy War—each a bargain. Five volumes would neatly fill
that gap on your second shelf. It looks rather untidy, does it not, sir?”
His remark was so precise that I instinctively turned to glance at the cabinet behind me.
That single movement altered everything.
When I looked back, the old man had vanished.
In his place stood Sherlock Holmes—smiling calmly across my study table.
For several seconds, I could neither speak nor move. Then the room seemed to darken; a grey
mist swirled before my eyes, and I lost all sense of awareness.
When I recovered, I found myself seated, my collar loosened, the sharp taste of brandy
lingering. Holmes stood over me, a flask in his hand.
“My dear Watson,” he said in that familiar voice, “I owe you a thousand apologies. I had not
anticipated that my reappearance would affect you so strongly.”
I seized him by the arms.
“Holmes!” I cried. “Is it truly you? Can you indeed be alive? Did you escape that dreadful
abyss?”
“Pray, compose yourself,” he replied. “Are you certain you are fit to discuss such matters? I fear
my return has been unnecessarily dramatic.”

“I am quite well,” I said, though my voice trembled. “But I can scarcely trust my senses. To
think that you—of all men—should stand here before me...”
Holmes regarded me steadily, a faint smile still upon his lips.
“Appearances,” he said quietly, “are often deceptive, my dear Watson.”
He paused.
“And what you have seen today—”
He did not finish.

Doyle.

Lockhart and Fort Gulistan, stood the modest post of Saragarhi—isolated, exposed, yet crucial.
Manned by just twenty-one soldiers under Havildar Ishar Singh, it served as a vital
communication link between the two forts. In a region where visibility itself was a challenge,
their duty was not merely functional—it was a responsibility carried in the name of their
regiment and their honour.
The vulnerability of Saragarhi soon became evident. After failing to capture nearby positions,
a massive tribal force turned toward this small post. Surrounded and cut off from
reinforcements, supplies, and retreat, the defenders were left with only one advantage: their

unwavering resolve. They knew that holding Saragarhi was not just about ground—it was
about upholding duty against impossible odds.
The attack began on the morning of 12 September. The defenders repelled the first assault, but
the imbalance was stark. While the attackers returned in waves, the defenders could only
endure, their numbers steadily thinning. Yet, no thought of surrender found place among
them.
As the battle intensified, the attackers resorted to strategy—offering terms, then setting fire to
the surrounding brush. Smoke engulfed the post, and under its cover, a breach was forced into
the wall. The defenders split their already meagre strength to contain it, weakening their
position further.
Inside, resistance turned into resolve of a higher order. Messages continued to flash to Fort
Lockhart even as the walls began to fall. When the moment came, Sepoy Gurmukh Singh sent
his final signal and chose to join the fight—not because victory was certain, but because duty

questions.stimulus:
Il.	The Last Stand at Saragarhi: In September 1897, on a rugged frontier between Fort
Lockhart and Fort Gulistan, stood the modest post of Saragarhi—isolated, exposed, yet crucial.
Manned by just twenty-one soldiers under Havildar Ishar Singh, it served as a vital
communication link between the two forts. In a region where visibility itself was a challenge,
their duty was not merely functional—it was a responsibility carried in the name of their
regiment and their honour.
The vulnerability of Saragarhi soon became evident. After failing to capture nearby positions,
a massive tribal force turned toward this small post. Surrounded and cut off from
reinforcements, supplies, and retreat, the defenders were left with only one advantage: their

unwavering resolve. They knew that holding Saragarhi was not just about ground—it was
about upholding duty against impossible odds.
The attack began on the morning of 12 September. The defenders repelled the first assault, but
the imbalance was stark. While the attackers returned in waves, the defenders could only
endure, their numbers steadily thinning. Yet, no thought of surrender found place among
them.
As the battle intensified, the attackers resorted to strategy—offering terms, then setting fire to
the surrounding brush. Smoke engulfed the post, and under its cover, a breach was forced into
the wall. The defenders split their already meagre strength to contain it, weakening their
position further.
Inside, resistance turned into resolve of a higher order. Messages continued to flash to Fort
Lockhart even as the walls began to fall. When the moment came, Sepoy Gurmukh Singh sent
his final signal and chose to join the fight—not because victory was certain, but because duty
demanded nothing less.www.lawpreptutorial.com
What followed was not merely a battle, but a testament.
The wounded rose again. The outnumbered stood firm. One by one, the defenders fell—but
none yielded. They fought not for survival, but for something greater than themselves.
By the time silence descended upon Saragarhi, the post had fallen—but its defenders had
ensured that their sacrifice would endure, not as loss, but as a lasting expression of courage,
honour, and an unyielding sense of belonging to something larger than life.
Source: Excerpt with edits - the historical event known as the Battle of Saragarhi, involving
soldiers of the 36th Sikh Regiment

Ill.	When Power Expands—and Must Return: The Constitution of India recognises that
moments of grave crisis may demand responses that go beyond ordinary governance. Under
Article 352, the President may proclaim an Emergency when the security of the nation is
threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. Significantly, this power may be
exercised even before the threat fully materialises, provided there exists an imminent danger.
In doing so, the Constitution attempts to anticipate instability rather than merely react to it.
Yet, this expansion of authority is not left to individual judgment. The decision must arise
from the Union Cabinet, ensuring that such a step reflects collective responsibility. Further,
the proclamation cannot continue indefinitely without parliamentary approval. Within a
defined period, both Houses must endorse it, failing which it automatically lapses. Even after
approval, its continuation depends on periodic review, embedding a rhythm of accountability
within an otherwise extraordinary measure.

During an Emergency, the balance of power shifts. The Union may direct States and legislate
on matters beyond its usual domain, and certain freedoms may be restricted. However, these
changes do not dismantle the constitutional structure; they temporarily rearrange it. Power
does not escape the Constitution—it circulates differently within it.
At its most abstract, the Emergency framework reveals a deeper design: that the Constitution
prepares not only for order, but also for disorder, and in doing so, defines the limits of its own
flexibility. Authority, when stretched, is expected to remember the shape it must return to.
This expectation is reinforced through safeguards. The House of the People may disapprove
the proclamation, and even a fraction of its members can compel reconsideration. Thus, the
system ensures that even at its most powerful, the State remains answerable.
Source: Excerpt with edits - Constitution of India, particularly Article 352 (National
Emergency).

questions.stimulus:
IV.	When Pope Leo XIV announced that his first pastoral visit would be to Lebanon, the response
among many residents was marked by a mixture of anticipation and unease. The country, still
recovering from recent conflict and marked by a long history of sectarian violence, exists in a
state where the expectation of instability is deeply ingrained. Even periods of calm are often
perceived not as peace, but as temporary interruptions in an otherwise continuous cycle of
conflict.
Lebanon presents a paradox. It is widely regarded as a symbol of interreligious coexistence,
with political power formally distributed among different religious communities and physical
spaces reflecting this diversity. Mosques and churches stand in close proximity, and divisions
that once defined the city have, at least superficially, faded. Yet beneath this appearance of
unity lies a persistent anxiety shaped by historical memory and recurring violence.

The Pope’s visit, therefore, was not merely a religious event but also a symbolic gesture. It
brought attention to Lebanon’s role as both a site of coexistence and a locus of ongoing crisis.
While such visits are typically interpreted as affirmations of hope and renewal, in Lebanon
they carry an additional dimension: they momentarily suspend the anticipation of conflict
without necessarily altering its underlying causes.
This tension is further reflected in the everyday experiences of those living in the country.
Public expressions of welcome and unity coexist with the constant presence of military activity
and the awareness that stability may be fragile. Even as large gatherings celebrate messages
of peace, the sounds of conflict persist in the background, reinforcing a sense that normalcy is
provisional.
In this context, the idea of peace itself becomes ambiguous. It is not experienced as a stable
condition but as something deferred—an aspiration rather than a reality. The departure of
symbolic figures such as the Pope does not resolve this tension; rather, it often marks a return
to familiar uncertainties. Thus, Lebanon’s condition challenges conventional understandings of
peace, suggesting that in some contexts, peace may exist less as a state of being and more as a
momentary reprieve.
Source: Excerpt with edits - The Point Magazine, discussing Lebanon in the context of a papal
visit.

cultures, alchemists, botanists, chemists and biologists over centuries. The discovery that
linked biology to chemistry was Louis Pasteur’s demonstration that living yeast cells are
responsible for the fermentation of sugar into alcohol in the absence of oxygen. Today, crops

many medicines that do not mix well with water; and in liquid pain medications, cough and
cold medicines. It helps keep medicines mixed and stable and also acts as a preservative. It is
also used in mouthwashes, perfumes, deodorants, paints, and markers
As a fuel and fuel additive, it has a 200-year history. In 1826, American inventor Samuel
Morey developed an engine that ran on ethanol and turpentine. In 1860, Nicholas Otto, a
German engineer best known for developing the modern internal combustion engine, used
ethanol as the fuel in one of his engines. In 1896, Henry Ford built his first automobile, the
quadricycle, to run on pure ethanol. In 1908, he produced the flexible fuel Model T that could
run on ethanol, gasoline, or a combination of both. Ethanol was also an important fuel for early
rockets and is still used in some lightweight rocket-powered aircraft.

IX.	At 89 seconds from midnight according to the doomsday clock and after [N] years of a
moratorium on nuclear testing, the United States President, Donald Trump, announced that
the U.S. would be resuming nuclear weapons testing. This adds yet another confusing and
alarming policy to a growing assortment of such policies under Mr. Trump’s belt.
The timing of the announcement is not coincidental. Mr. Trump’s post, on Truth Social, came
after Russia announced the successful test of a ‘nuclear-capable cruise missile’. It also came
the same day as Mr. Trump’s meeting with China’s President Xi Jinping. Given the current
state of the international order, the implications of this move are likely to be widespread.
Speculation about the beginning of another arms race has already begun and the state of the
global nuclear non-proliferation architecture is likely to be determined by what happens in the
months ahead. While the details of what kind of testing the U.S. intends to carry out are
unclear, this is likely to be perceived as a massive shift in U.S. nuclear posturing.
On the obvious power equations, U.S.-China and U.S.-Russia dynamics are likely to be directly
impacted. Since the announcement on testing, a spokesperson from China’s Foreign Ministry
has urged the U.S. to ‘abide by its commitments to the comprehensive nuclear test-ban treaty
(CTBTY.

If the U.S. fails to do so, China and Russia could both potentially resume their nuclear testing.
It would allow them to try out new and advanced weapons (such as low yield ‘tactical’ nuclear
weapons), without being held responsible for being the ones to break the moratorium.
The New START Treaty, which limits the number of strategic warheads and delivery vehicles
that the U.S. and Russia can deploy, will expire in February [YYYY]. If the U.S. resumes
testing, a successor agreement will become even more challenging to negotiate. Coming to the
less obvious implications of the resumption of nuclear testing, 50 years of nuclear arms
controls are now likely to be under strain. While the CTBT never entered into force, the
moratorium on testing served like a tacit agreement, which all major powers (apart from North
Korea) have voluntarily abided by since the 1990s. Now, as the U.S. sets a precedent for
breaking the moratorium, other countries apart from China and Russia could use this as
justification for conducting their own nuclear tests.

attacked V — each acting on his own separate impulse after being independently provoked by

Section 103 read with Section 3(5) BNS, arguing that since both attacked the same victim at

simultaneous action at the same place and time, without proof of a prior meeting of minds,

Simultaneous action by two persons against the same victim at the same time and place

options.label: d

similar intention; mere simultaneous or coincidental acts do not establish such shared
intention.

A gang of four people planned to rob a jewellery shop. Three entered the shop, threatened the
owner at gunpoint, and looted the cash. The fourth, P, stood at the entrance as a lookout,

P is liable only for robbery and not for murder, because the killing was not part of the

the use of deadly force before the robbery commenced; murder, requiring specific intent,
cannot be imputed to a participant merely from his facilitative role.

options.label: c
options.text:
P is liable for murder under Section 3(5) because he actively participated in furtherance of
the common plan by acting as a lookout, and the killing occurred during the execution of
that shared plan.

questions.stem:
Eight persons, including R, formed a group armed with lathis and iron rods and marched to
the house of a rival with the common object of demolishing his property. During the course of
the incident, when the rival resisted, one member of the group stabbed him with a knife,
causing his death. There was no prior discussion among the members about killing anyone. R
contended that he only intended to assist in demolition and had no knowledge that any
member would commit murder. The trial court convicted all members under Section 103 read
with Section 190 BNS. On appeal, the question is whether R can be held liable for murder
under Section 190 despite absence of prior discussion regarding killing.

options.label: a
options.text:
R is not liable for murder because he personally carried only a lathi and had no intention to
cause death; Section 190 requires proof of individual intention for the specific offence
charged.

options.label: b
options.text:
R can only be convicted for rioting under Section 191(1) BNS because his personal object
was limited to demolition and not murder in this case; liability cannot extend beyond the
accused's own declared purpose.

options.label: c
options.text:
R's liability under Section 190 depends on whether he individually participated in the
stabbing; since he was not directly involved, he cannot be held liable for murder.

options.label: d
options.text:
R is liable under Section 190 as a member of the unlawful assembly when the offence was
committed; the murder was either in prosecution of the common object or was one the
members knew was likely.

Five persons were charged under Section 103 read with Section 190 BNS for the murder of V.
During trial, two accused were acquitted as the prosecution failed to prove their participation in the
unlawful assembly. The remaining three accused were convicted under Section 103 read with
Section 190 BNS. On appeal, the defence argued that with fewer than five persons found to share
the common object, Section 190 could not be applied. The prosecution contended that even if Section
190 fails, the conviction can be sustained under Section 103 read with Section 3(5) BNS on the
same evidence. The question is whether the conviction under Section 190 can stand and whether
Section 3(5) may be applied in its place.

options.label: a
b
options.text:
The conviction under Section 190 fails once the common object is shared by fewer than five
persons; Section 3(5) may apply if common intention is established and no prejudice is caused to
the accused.

options.label: c
options.text:
The conviction under Section 190 remains valid so long as at least two persons are convicted,
since an unlawful assembly may lawfully consist of fewer than five members after the court
returns its findings.

options.label: d
options.text:
The accused must be acquitted entirely since Section 3(5) cannot be invoked at the appellate
stage where no specific charge was framed against them at the time of trial.

questions.stem:
Seven persons assembled with the common object of forcibly occupying a piece of disputed
agricultural land. Armed with lathis, they proceeded to the field. On reaching the land, one
member, without any prior discussion, drew out a country-made pistol — which no other member
knew he was carrying — and fired it, fatally injuring the landowner. The remaining six members
had no prior knowledge of the firearm. All seven were charged under Section 103 read with Section
190 BNS. The six surviving members argued that the common object was forcible occupation, not
murder, and that they had no knowledge that any member carried a firearm or intended to shoot
anyone. The Sessions Court acquitted all six under the first limb of Section 190 but convicted them
under the second limb on the ground that violence was a foreseeable consequence of an armed
assembly. The question before the High Court is whether the second limb of Section 190 is correctly
applied.

options.label: a
options.text:
All seven members are liable for murder under the first limb of Section 190 because killing the
landowner was directly in prosecution of the common object of occupying the land; his removal
was a necessary step, making the murder inseparable from the shared objective.

options.label: b
options.text:
The six members may be liable under the second limb of Section 190 only if, given all the
circumstances, it was reasonably inferable that a member was likely to commit murder
specifically; a generalised foreseeing of violence or disorder is insufficient to satisfy the
knowledge requirement.

options.label: c
options.text:
The six members are entirely exempt from liability for murder because the shooting was an
independent act unconnected with the common object; the second limb of Section 190 requires
knowledge of the likelihood of the specific offence, which cannot be inferred where no member
knew of the firearm.

options.label: d
options.text:
Section 190 imposes absolute vicarious liability on every member of an unlawful assembly for
all acts committed during the assembly; since all seven were present when the fatal shot was
fired, they are collectively liable for murder without any further inquiry into individual
knowledge.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) are the two principal doctrines of constructive or joint
criminal liability. Both provisions impose criminal liability on each member of a group for an
act committed by any member, but they differ substantially in their requirements and
operation.
Section 3(5) BNS provides that when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance
of the common intention of all, each person is liable as if the act were done by him alone.
Section 3(5) is not a substantive offence but a rule of joint liability that operates in conjunction
with another penal provision. Its essential ingredients are: (i) a criminal act done by several
persons; (ii) existence of a common intention shared by all; and (iii) participation in the act in
furtherance of that common intention. Mahbub Shah v. Emperor emphasised that common
intention implies prior concert and is distinct from similar intention, which is merely a
simultaneous inclination of several persons acting independently. However, such a meeting of
minds need not involve lengthy premeditation and may crystallise on the spot in response to
developing circumstances.
Active participation in the criminal act is a necessary element of Section 3(5). Mere presence at
the scene is insufficient to attract liability. However, participation need not take the form of
direct physical commission of the offence; assistance, instigation, or facilitation at the scene in
furtherance of the pre-arranged plan suffices. In Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. King Emperor
(1925), the Privy Council held that an accused who stood guard outside a post office while his
associates entered and killed the postmaster during a robbery was jointly liable for murder
under Section 3(5), since he was present and participating in furtherance of the common plan
even though he did not personally fire the shot. The principle that "the act of one is the act of
all" applies where participation in furtherance of the plan is established.
Section 190 BNS operates on a different basis. It provides that every member of an unlawful
assembly is guilty of any offence committed by any member of that assembly in prosecution of
the common object, or of such offences as the members knew were likely to be committed in
prosecution of that object. An unlawful assembly is defined under Section 189 BNS as an
assembly of five or more persons sharing a common object of one of the enumerated kinds.
Section 190 does not require proof of a prior meeting of minds; membership in the unlawful
assembly at the time the offence is committed is sufficient to attract vicarious liability. In Lalji
v. State of U.P. (1989), the Supreme Court held that the crucial inquiry is whether the accused
was a member of the unlawful assembly at the relevant time and whether the offence was
committed in prosecution of the common object or with knowledge that it was likely to be
committed.

Section 190 contains two distinct limbs: (i) liability for offences committed in prosecution of the
common object; and (ii) liability for offences which members knew were likely to be committed.
The Supreme Court in Mizaji v. State of U.P. (1959) clarified that knowledge under the second
limb must be of the likelihood of the specific offence, assessed objectively from the
circumstances — not a vague awareness of possible disorder.
A critical distinction between Sections 3(5) and 190 is that the former requires active
participation while the latter imposes liability on the basis of membership alone. Under
Section 190, if the number of members of the unlawful assembly is reduced below five owing to
acquittals, the remaining accused cannot be convicted under Section 190 unless Section 3(5)
independently applies. The Supreme Court in Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab (1963) held that
Section 190 cannot be applied where fewer than five persons are found to have shared the
common object. Sections 3(5) and 190 are not mutually exclusive; courts have recognised that
Section 3(5) may be applied in place of Section 190 where evidence establishes common
intention, provided the accused suffered no prejudice in their defence.

questions.stem:
A and B, friends, went together to confront C over a financial dispute. There was no prior plan to assault
C. When C made an insulting remark, A spontaneously struck C with his fists. C, physically stronger,
began to overpower A. B, who had not previously discussed violence, immediately picked up a heavy
stone lying nearby and struck C on the head, fatally injuring him. B argued before the Sessions Court
that since there was no pre-arranged plan to cause harm when they set out to meet C, no common
intention existed and Section 3(5) should not apply. The Sessions Court convicted both under Section 103
read with Section 3(5) BNS. On appeal, the question is whether common intention under Section 3(5) can
crystallise on the spot in the course of a confrontation that was not originally planned as a violent
encounter.

options.label: a
options.text:
Common intention under Section 8(5) may crystallise on the spot in response to developing
circumstances; if A and B shared a common intention to cause harm at the moment B intervened,
both are liable under Section 3(5) even in the absence of prior premeditation.

options.label: b
options.text:
Common intention under Section 3(5) can only be established by evidence of a plan formed well
before the incident; an intention that develops spontaneously at the scene does not constitute
common intention within the meaning of Section 3(5), as the provision contemplates forethought.

options.label: c
options.text:
Section 3(5) does not apply because A and B originally went only to confront C verbally; any violence
that ensued was beyond their initial purpose, making it an independent act of each individual
outside the scope of the joint plan originally formed.

options.label: d
options.text:
B is independently liable for murder under Section 103, but A cannot be held liable under Section
3(5) for B's act because A was unarmed; Section 3(5) requires each participant to use the same type
or category of force as the person who commits the fatal act.

questions.stem:
Five persons were tried for the murder of V, charged under Section 103 read with Section 190 BNS.
During trial, two accused were acquitted as the prosecution failed to prove their membership in the
unlawful assembly. The remaining three — X, Y, and Z — were convicted under Section 103 read with
Section 190 BNS. On appeal before the High Court, the defence argued that with only three persons
found to share the common object, Section 190 was inapplicable and the convictions must be set aside
entirely. The prosecution argued in the alternative that the same evidence established a clear common
intention among X, Y, and Z to commit murder, and requested the court to apply Section 3(5) instead.
The question before the High Court is whether X, Y, and Z may be convicted under Section 103 read with
Section 3(5) BNS when they were originally charged only under Section 103 read with Section 190 BNS,
and whether the court may apply Section 3(5) for the first time at the appellate stage.

options.label: a
options.text:
X, Y, and Z cannot be convicted under Section 3(5) at the appellate stage because they were charged
and tried under Section 190; substituting the mode of liability at the appellate stage without a fresh
charge violates the constitutional guarantee that every accused must be informed of the specific
charge against him.

options.label: b
options.text:
The court must acquit X, Y, and Z entirely; since Section 190 is inapplicable due to the reduction
below five members, and Section 3(5) was never charged, the court has no jurisdiction to convict on
an uncharged mode of liability at the appellate stage.

options.label: c
options.text:
Section 3(5) may be applied by the appellate court in place of Section 190 where the evidence on
record independently establishes common intention and active participation among the remaining
accused, provided the accused suffered no prejudice in their defence by the absence of a specific
Section 3(5) charge.

options.label: d
options.text:
Since the substantive offence — murder under Section 103 — remains the same regardless of
whether Section 3(5) or Section 190 is the operative mode of joint liability, the appellate court must
uphold the conviction on the basis of each accused's individual presence at the scene, without
requiring the prosecution to establish either provision afresh.

XII. Free Consent under the Indian Contract Act, 1872: Section 14 of the Indian Contract Act,
1872 provides that consent is free only when not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud,
misrepresentation, or mistake. A contract with vitiated consent is either void or voidable
depending on the cause.
Coercion under Section 15 involves threatening to commit an IPC-forbidden act or unlawfully
detaining property to compel a contract. In Chikham Amiraju v. Chikham Seshamma, a threat
to commit suicide was held to constitute coercion. Such contracts are voidable at the option of
the aggrieved party.
Undue influence under Section 16 arises where one party dominates the other's will — through
authority, fiduciary position, or the other's diminished capacity — and uses it to obtain an
unfair advantage. Once dominance is established, the burden shifts to the stronger party to
prove the transaction was not unconscionable.
Fraud under Section 17 requires a knowingly false representation made to deceive. Mere
silence is not fraud unless a duty to speak exists. Fraudulently induced contracts are voidable
and additionally ground a damages claim.
Misrepresentation under Section 18 is an honest but false assertion of fact that induces the
contract. No intent to deceive is required. Such contracts are voidable but do not independently
give rise to damages. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Under Section 20, a bilateral mistake of fact essential to the agreement renders the contract
void. A unilateral mistake under Section 22 does not ordinarily affect validity. Mistake of law
under Section 21 is no ground for avoidance.
Source: Extracted with revisions and modifications from:
K.D. Gaur, Textbook on Indian Contract Law; and relevant case law including Chikham
Amiraju v. Chikham Seshamma (1917).
questions.stem:
A moneylender who managed an elderly widow's deceased son's accounts persuaded her to
mortgage her only house at 48% interest. She had no financial literacy and received no
independent advice. She later challenged the mortgage on grounds of undue influence.

options.label: a
options.text:
Since she signed the mortgage voluntarily, her consent is conclusively presumed free
regardless of surrounding circumstances; the presence of financial illiteracy or absence of
independent advice does not vitiate consent once the signature is established.

options.label: b
options.text:
No undue influence arises as no formal fiduciary relationship such as trustee-beneficiary
existed between the parties; Section 16 requires a legally recognised position of authority
which a mere moneylender does not occupy.

options.label: c
options.text:
The widow must independently prove both dominance and absence of independent advice
to establish undue influence; the burden never shifts to the stronger party under Section
16 as each element must be established by the weaker party throughout.

options.label: d
options.text:
The moneylender was in a position to dominate her will and used that position to gain an
unfair advantage. Therefore, the transaction may be presumed to be induced by undue
influence, and the burden lies on the moneylender to prove otherwise.

questions.stem:
A seller told a buyer that a horse was "perfectly sound" knowing it suffered from recurring
lameness. The buyer purchased it relying on this statement and later sought rescission and
damages when the condition appeared.

options.label: a
options.text:
The statement is misrepresentation under Section 18; the buyer may rescind but cannot
claim damages as there was no fraudulent intent.

options.label: b
options.text:
The buyer has no remedy as caveat emptor applies where the buyer had an opportunity to
inspect.

options.label: c
options.text:
The statement is fraud as it was made with knowledge of its falsity to induce the contract;
the buyer may rescind and claim damages.

options.label: d
options.text: The statement is mere sales puffery with no legal consequences under the Contract Act.

questions.stem:
A landlord threatened his tenant that unless the tenant signed a lease renewal at triple the
original rent, he would file a false criminal complaint against the tenant's son. The tenant
signed under this threat and later sought to avoid the contract on grounds of coercion.

options.label: a
options.text:
The contract is void, not voidable, because coercion involves a threat of criminal action
which renders the consent entirely absent rather than merely defective.

options.label: b
options.text:
This constitutes coercion as threatening to file a false complaint to compel consent amounts
to threatening a forbidden act; the contract is voidable at the tenant's option.

options.label: c
options.text:
Since the tenant had an option to refuse and approach the courts, the threat does not
constitute coercion; free consent requires only that no physical force was used.

options.label: d
options.text:
This is not coercion under Section 15 as threatening a criminal complaint does not
constitute an act forbidden by the IPC; coercion requires physical compulsion to be present.

questions.stem:
A agreed to sell a specific parcel of land to B for construction of a warehouse. Both parties
believed that the land measured 10,000 square feet, based on an old survey map relied upon
during negotiations. After execution of the agreement, it was discovered through an official re-
survey that the land actually measured only 6,000 square feet, substantially reducing its
suitability for the intended purpose. B sought to avoid the contract on the ground of mistake.
The question is whether the agreement is affected by mistake under the Indian Contract Act,
1872.

options.label: a
options.text:
The contract is valid because the mistake relates only to the quantity of the land, which
does not affect the validity of the agreement unless expressly made a condition of the
contract.

options.label: b
options.text:
The contract is voidable at B’s option because the mistake materially affected the value of
the subject matter, and any such mistake renders the contract voidable.

options.label: c
options.text:
The contract is void as both parties were under a bilateral mistake of fact essential to the
agreement ie., the identity and extent of the subject matter.

options.label: d
options.text:
The contract is valid because a mistake as to area is a unilateral mistake, and only one
party can rely on it to avoid the contract.

questions.stem:
A supplier entered into a contract with a company for supply of raw materials. During
negotiations, the company’s agent stated that “the company’s standard payment cycle is
30 days, and all suppliers are paid within that period.” Relying on this statement, the
supplier agreed to the contract. However, the written agreement provided for a 90-day
payment period, which the supplier did not notice at the time of signing. The agent
genuinely believed the statement to be true but was mistaken.
The supplier later sought to avoid the contract on the ground of misrepresentation.

options.label: a
options.text:
The statement constitutes fraud under Section 17 as any incorrect statement inducing a
contract amounts to fraud irrespective of intent; the supplier may therefore rescind the
contract and additionally claim damages for the loss suffered.

options.label: b
options.text:
The contract is valid because the supplier had the opportunity to read the written
agreement and is bound by its terms; a party who fails to exercise due diligence at the time
of signing cannot subsequently seek avoidance on grounds of misrepresentation.

options.label: c
options.text:
The statement constitutes misrepresentation under Section 18 as an honest but false
assertion of fact that induced the contract; the contract is voidable at the supplier's option
since the agent's genuine belief does not cure the falsity of the representation.

options.label: d
options.text:
The statement is merely an expression of opinion regarding business practice and does not
amount to any representation of fact; no actionable misrepresentation arises where the
party merely describes a general commercial practice without asserting it as a contractual
term.

A person signed a surety agreement believing, due to his own misreading, that he was signing
a guarantee for Rs. 10,000 when the document stated Rs. 1,00,000. No one misled him. He
later sought to avoid the contract claiming unilateral mistake.

options.label: a
options.text:
The contract is voidable at the option of the disadvantaged party under Section 22 as
unilateral mistake vitiates consent when it relates to the amount — a fundamental term.

options.label: b
options.text:
The contract is void under Section 20 as the party was clearly mistaken about the essential
terms of the agreement.

options.label: c
options.text:
The contract is valid as unilateral mistake does not ordinarily affect the validity of the
contract; no other party caused or contributed to the mistake.

however caused, is a mistake of fact essential to the agreement under Section 20.

questions.stimulus:
XIII. Torts Against Property: Trespass to land is a direct, intentional interference with another's
possession of land without lawful justification. It is actionable per se — no proof of damage is
required. The tort protects possessory rights; even a person in wrongful possession may sue a
trespasser. Trespass may be committed by physical entry, placing objects on the land, or
remaining after permission is withdrawn. Mistaken belief that one owns or has permission to
enter the land is no defence.
Private nuisance is an indirect, unreasonable interference with a person's use and enjoyment
of land. Unlike trespass, damage must generally be proved. Reasonableness is assessed by
balancing the gravity of the interference, its duration, the character of the neighbourhood, and
the utility of the defendant's conduct. The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) imposes strict
liability where a person brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes, and it
does escape and cause damage. The defendant is liable even without negligence, subject to the
defences of act of God, act of a stranger, and the plaintiff's own default.
The doctrine of distress damage feasant entitles a landowner to seize and detain chattels —
animals or objects — found on his land causing damage, until compensation is paid. The right
is possessory only; the distrainor cannot sell or destroy the chattel. The right is lost once the
chattel leaves the land voluntarily.
The rule against extra-sensitive plaintiffs in property torts mirrors the general principle: a
defendant is not liable for damage that would not have occurred but for the abnormal
sensitivity of the plaintiff's property or use. Where ordinary land or property would not have
suffered the harm complained of, a defendant conducting a reasonable activity is not liable
merely because the plaintiff's particular use is unusually delicate. This principle was applied
in Robinson v. Kilvert (1889), where heat from the defendant's operations damaged the
plaintiff's unusually sensitive brown paper stored in the premises above, but would not have
affected ordinary goods; the court denied relief.
Conversion is the wrongful dealing with another's chattel in a manner inconsistent with the
owner's right to possession — including taking, destroying, selling, or retaining it without
authority. The plaintiff must have a possessory title at the time of the act. Conversion is
actionable per se and entitles the plaintiff to the full value of the chattel.

including Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) and Robinson v. Kilvert (1889).
questions.stem:
A farmer's cattle strayed onto a neighbour's field, grazed on crops, and were seized by the
neighbour before they wandered off. The neighbour refused to return the cattle until the
farmer paid for the crop damage. The farmer argued the seizure was unlawful as the cattle
had caused no substantial harm.

options.label: a
options.text:
The seizure is unlawful; distress damage feasant requires the distrainor to first obtain a
court order before detaining another's animals.

options.label: b
options.text:
The seizure is unlawful because the cattle were animals capable of independent movement;

D is not liable because he exercised reasonable care; the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher does

D is liable only if the plaintiff proves D knew of the crack; strict liability under Rylands v.

D is strictly liable under Rylands v. Fletcher; industrial solvent stored in large quantities

questions.stimulus:
XIV. Right to Die with Dignity under Article 21 of the Constitution of India: Article 21 of
the Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except
according to procedure established by law. Through successive judicial interpretation, the
Supreme Court has examined whether this right extends to a choice to end one's life or to die
with dignity.
In P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994), a two-judge bench struck down Section 309 IPC,
which criminalised attempted suicide, holding that just as the right to freedom of speech
includes the right to remain silent, the right to life under Article 21 includes the right not to
live. The Court reasoned that punishing a person who has already suffered mental agony by
attempting suicide is cruel and unconstitutional.
In Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996), a five-judge Constitution Bench overruled P.
Rathinam. The Court held that the right to life under Article 21 does not include the right to
die. The Court held that the right to life does not include a right to terminate life prematurely;
the right to live with dignity extends throughout the natural course of life but does not
encompass its artificial termination. The Court upheld Sections 306 and 309 IPC as
constitutionally valid. Crucially, however, the Court also observed that the right to live with
dignity may include, for a terminally ill patient, the right to a dignified process of dying —
leaving open the door for future recognition of euthanasia.
In Aruna Ramachandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011), the Supreme Court
recognised that passive euthanasia — withdrawal or withholding of life-sustaining treatment
— may be permitted in exceptional circumstances. The Court held that active euthanasia
remained impermissible, but passive euthanasia for patients in a Persistent Vegetative State
(PVS) could be authorised by a High Court through a bench of at least two judges, following
consultation with a medical board. This decision drew on the observation in Gian Kaur that
dignified dying is part of Article 21.
In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), a five-judge Constitution Bench unequivocally
held that the right to die with dignity is an intrinsic facet of the right to life under Article 21.
The Court formalised the legality of passive euthanasia and, for the first time, recognised the
validity of Advance Medical Directives (living wills), allowing competent individuals to specify
in advance their refusal of life-prolonging treatment. The Court grounded this in individual
autonomy, bodily integrity, and self-determination as components of Article 21, and laid down
comprehensive procedural safeguards. Active euthanasia remained illegal.
In Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026), the Supreme Court applied the Common Cause
framework to permit withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition from a patient who had been in
a persistent vegetative state since 2012. The bench observed that prolonging mere biological
existence in the absence of any prospect of recovery does not serve the patient's best interests,
and that human dignity at the end of life is a legally protected value under Article 21.

decisions including P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994), Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996),
Aruna Ramachandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011), Common Cause v. Union of India
(2018), and Harish Rana v. Union of India (2026).
questions.stem:
A terminally ill patient with no prospect of recovery was being kept alive by ventilator support.
His family sought enforcement of his earlier oral statements that he never wished to be kept
on artificial life support. The hospital refused to withdraw treatment absent a court order,
citing uncertainty over the law. The family's counsel argued that under Common Cause (2018),
the patient's advance wishes constituted a binding living will.
The question is whether an oral statement of treatment refusal qualifies as a valid Advance
Medical Directive under the Common Cause framework.

options.label: a
options.text:
An oral statement of treatment refusal constitutes a valid Advance Medical Directive, as
the right to self-determination under Article 21 cannot be restricted by procedural
formalities requiring written documentation.

options.label: b
options.text:
Any clearly expressed prior wish of a patient, whether oral or written, must be treated as
binding under Article 21 once the right to die with dignity is recognised as a fundamental
right.

options.label: c
options.text:
An oral directive may be treated as valid if it is supported by consistent testimony of family
members and doctors, as procedural safeguards are intended to ensure authenticity rather
than mandate form.

options.label: d
options.text:
An Advance Medical Directive must be in writing and executed with prescribed safeguards
by a competent adult, and an oral statement does not satisfy these requirements under the
Common Cause framework.

questions.stem:
A couple was convicted under Section 306 IPC for abetting their daughter-in-law's suicide. On
appeal before the Constitution Bench, they argued that if the right to life includes the right to
die, abetting a constitutionally protected act cannot be an offence. They further argued that
Section 306 and Section 309 IPC stand and fall together — if one is unconstitutional, the other
must also be invalid.
The question is whether Section 306 IPC can survive independently of Section 309 IPC.

options.label: a
options.text:
Section 306 and Section 309 IPC are inseparably linked, such that if the offence of attempt
to suicide is held unconstitutional, the offence of abetment of suicide must also necessarily
become invalid.

options.label: b
options.text:
Section 306 IPC creates a distinct offence that survives independently of Section 309 IPC,
as abetment of suicide punishes third-party conduct and is not dependent on the
criminality of the principal act.

options.label: c
options.text:
Section 309 IPC may be valid while Section 306 remains constitutionally suspect, since
abetment involves a third party’s role and raises different considerations relating to
individual autonomy and criminal liability.

options.label: d
options.text:
If suicide or its attempt is not punishable, abetment of suicide cannot be treated as an
offence, because criminal liability for abetment must necessarily depend upon the
punishability of the principal act itself.

questions.stem:
A competent adult suffering from progressive motor neurone disease executed a document titled
"Advance Medical Directive" stating she did not wish to be placed on ventilator support if she lost
capacity to breathe independently. She signed the document before two witnesses, both of whom
attested it. However, she did not present the document to a Judicial Magistrate for
countersignature as required under the Common Cause framework. Several months later she lost
capacity and doctors proposed ventilator support. Her family sought enforcement of the directive.
The hospital contended it was not validly executed.
The question before the court is whether a written directive signed by the patient and attested by
witnesses, but lacking the mandatory Judicial Magistrate countersignature, constitutes a valid
Advance Medical Directive under the Common Cause framework.

options.label: a
options.text:
The directive is valid; the Judicial Magistrate countersignature is a procedural formality
designed to assist authentication, and substantial compliance with the remaining requirements
suffices to give effect to the patient's clearly expressed autonomous will.

options.label: b
options.text:
The directive is valid because the patient was mentally competent at the time of execution and
the document reflects her genuine and informed wishes; courts should give effect to the spirit of
the Common Cause framework rather than requiring strict adherence to each procedural step.

options.label: c
options.text:
The directive is invalid; the procedural requirements laid down in Common Cause — including
countersignature by a Judicial Magistrate — are mandatory safeguards, and non-compliance
with any of them renders the directive unenforceable.

options.label: d
options.text:
The directive may still be treated as valid evidence of the patient's wishes even if it does not
qualify as a formal Advance Medical Directive, since the right to self-determination under
Article 21 cannot be extinguished by procedural non-compliance.

questions.stem:
The family of a patient who had been in an irreversible coma for eight years petitioned the High
Court seeking authorisation for active euthanasia — specifically, the administration of a lethal
drug by a physician — arguing it was more humane than the prolonged withdrawal of nutrition and
hydration permitted under passive euthanasia. The family relied on the Common Cause judgment
and submitted that the constitutional right to die with dignity recognised in that case must
logically extend to active euthanasia as the more immediate and less distressing method of ending
life.
The High Court must determine whether active euthanasia is permissible under the constitutional
and legal framework as it currently stands in India.

options.label: a
options.text:
Active euthanasia is permissible where authorised by a High Court following procedural
safeguards applicable to passive euthanasia, since both involve a physician causing death and
the distinction between them is ethically arbitrary.

options.label: b
options.text:
Active euthanasia is permissible under Common Cause where the patient has been in an
irreversible coma for a prolonged period, as the "best interests" standard permits the most
humane available option.

options.label: c
options.text:
Active euthanasia remains impermissible under Indian law; the Supreme Court in both Aruna
Shanbaug and Common Cause expressly confined permissible euthanasia to passive euthanasia
and has not recognised active euthanasia.

options.label: d
options.text:
The distinction between active and passive euthanasia is not legally recognised in India; once a
court authorises termination of life on grounds of dignity, the method is a clinical matter left to
the treating physician.

questions.stem:
Harish Rana suffered severe brain injuries in 2012 and had been in a persistent vegetative
state for over a decade, sustained solely by clinically assisted nutrition. His family, unable to
bear his prolonged suffering, approached the Supreme Court seeking permission to withdraw
nutritional support, relying on the Common Cause framework. The hospital contended that
nutritional support was not a medical intervention and therefore could not be withdrawn
under passive euthanasia guidelines.

options.label: a
options.text:
Clinically assisted nutrition is basic care, not a medical intervention; withdrawing it
constitutes active euthanasia and remains impermissible regardless of the patient's
condition.

options.label: b
options.text:
Passive euthanasia under Common Cause is limited to withdrawal of mechanical
ventilation and does not extend to nutritional support; food and water constitute a
fundamental entitlement courts cannot authorise withdrawal of.

options.label: c
options.text:
Withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition from a patient in a persistent vegetative state
falls within permissible passive euthanasia, as prolonging existence without dignity does
not serve the patient's best interests.

options.label: d
options.text:
Withdrawal of any life-sustaining care requires an advance medical directive from the
patient; in the absence of a living will, the family's consent alone is insufficient to permit
withdrawal.

questions.stem:
A competent adult suffering from a terminal illness executed a written Advance Medical
Directive specifying that she did not wish to be placed on mechanical ventilation in the event
she lost capacity. A year later, she was hospitalised, lost the ability to communicate, and
doctors proposed ventilator support. The hospital sought legal clarity on whether the directive
was binding and whether withholding treatment in compliance with it would expose doctors to
criminal liability.

options.label: a
options.text:
Advance Medical Directives are merely advisory; doctors are not bound by them and must
administer all possible treatments in the patient's clinical interest.

options.label: b
options.text:
A directive refusing ventilator support is invalid because passive euthanasia always
requires fresh judicial approval at the time of withdrawal of treatment.

options.label: c
options.text:
A validly executed Advance Medical Directive is legally binding; doctors who act in
compliance with it and follow prescribed safeguards are protected from criminal liability.

options.label: d
options.text:
Advance Medical Directives are binding only on family members and not on treating
doctors, who remain independently bound by their professional duty to preserve life.

A patient's family executed a living will on her behalf claiming she had orally authorised them
to do so. The patient subsequently recovered partial consciousness but could not communicate.
The hospital refused to treat the living will as valid. The family argued that Common Cause
does not require the patient to personally execute the directive and that their authorisation
suffices.

options.label: a
options.text:
A living will may be executed by an immediate family member on behalf of a patient, as
they are the most appropriate persons to speak to the patient's best interests under the
"best interests" principle.

options.label: b
options.text:
An Advance Medical Directive must be executed by the individual personally while
competent; a directive executed by a family member in their place is invalid under the
Common Cause framework.

options.label: c
d
options.text:
Since the patient recovered partial consciousness, the living will — whether valid or not —
is superseded by the patient's current condition and cannot guide treatment decisions at
this stage.

SECTION IV
XVI. Historically and in the current day, our collective fascination with trees and forests, and by
corollary, our neglect of open grassy biomes has had very real consequences for how we have
come to understand, value and conserve the natural ecosystems around us.
Globally, as the extinction crisis of the past century has unfolded, scientific research and
conservation funding have been overwhelmingly focused on tropical rainforest diversity and
the crisis of tropical deforestation. So much have these majestic forested ecosystems dominated
our imagination that a formal term has been adopted for it, Biome Awareness Disparity
(BAD). BAD captures the idea that forested biomes have garnered more than their fair share
of attention, even as other, equally ancient biomes with their distinctive biodiversity, and in
the case of grasslands and savannas, unique and vibrant pastoral cultures, have been in plain
sight. Indeed, the rate of loss of open biomes both predates and outpaces rates of tropical
deforestation over the past century, but undervalued and perceived as “less than pristine”,
“degraded” systems, these losses have not garnered concern until very recently.
In India, as in many other parts of the tropics, these perceptions are historically entwined with
the advent of the colonial enterprise. Here in the subcontinent, the modern classification of
vegetation was formalised at the start of the colonial era. Colonial foresters, trained in forestry
traditions from densely forested, cooler climes, were charged with surveying the colonial lands,
with a special eye on timber, an important revenue source for the colonial state. In this tree-
centric lens, all ecosystems with some trees in them came to be classified as a type of “forest”.
Thus, while the densely wooded formations of mesic regions such as the central India or the
southern peninsula came to be classified as dry deciduous forests, the sparsely-treed
formations of the semi-arid regions of the Deccan and interior peninsula were classified as
thorn or scrub forests. But the visible presence of humans grazing their livestock herds across
these landscapes and setting dry-season fires to encourage fresh grass growth for their
livestock in the monsoon the followed, lent itself easily to the perception that these were
human-modified, degraded systems which in the absence of humans, would have been closed
forests. The more open and degraded of these regions, seen as unproductive in terms of
resource extraction, came to be administratively classified as “wastelands”. Further west
towards the desert, where there were vast grassy landscapes, it was clear that the region was
too arid to support trees, but these open landscapes, seasonally home to migrant pastoralists
and their herds, were also easily labelled as “wastelands”. This world view truly missed the
grasses for the absent trees. It failed to recognise that the productivity of these ecosystems lay
in the abundant grazing animals and livestock supported by the grass, and that the livestock
products they generated were the heart of a thriving economy based on adaptive and mobile
pastoralism. (science, 486 words)

SECTION IV
XVI. Historically and in the current day, our collective fascination with trees and forests, and by
corollary, our neglect of open grassy biomes has had very real consequences for how we have
come to understand, value and conserve the natural ecosystems around us.
Globally, as the extinction crisis of the past century has unfolded, scientific research and
conservation funding have been overwhelmingly focused on tropical rainforest diversity and
the crisis of tropical deforestation. So much have these majestic forested ecosystems dominated
our imagination that a formal term has been adopted for it, Biome Awareness Disparity
(BAD). BAD captures the idea that forested biomes have garnered more than their fair share
of attention, even as other, equally ancient biomes with their distinctive biodiversity, and in
the case of grasslands and savannas, unique and vibrant pastoral cultures, have been in plain
sight. Indeed, the rate of loss of open biomes both predates and outpaces rates of tropical
deforestation over the past century, but undervalued and perceived as “less than pristine”,
“degraded” systems, these losses have not garnered concern until very recently.
In India, as in many other parts of the tropics, these perceptions are historically entwined with
the advent of the colonial enterprise. Here in the subcontinent, the modern classification of
vegetation was formalised at the start of the colonial era. Colonial foresters, trained in forestry
traditions from densely forested, cooler climes, were charged with surveying the colonial lands,
with a special eye on timber, an important revenue source for the colonial state. In this tree-
centric lens, all ecosystems with some trees in them came to be classified as a type of “forest”.
Thus, while the densely wooded formations of mesic regions such as the central India or the
southern peninsula came to be classified as dry deciduous forests, the sparsely-treed
formations of the semi-arid regions of the Deccan and interior peninsula were classified as
thorn or scrub forests. But the visible presence of humans grazing their livestock herds across
these landscapes and setting dry-season fires to encourage fresh grass growth for their
livestock in the monsoon the followed, lent itself easily to the perception that these were
human-modified, degraded systems which in the absence of humans, would have been closed
forests. The more open and degraded of these regions, seen as unproductive in terms of
resource extraction, came to be administratively classified as “wastelands”. Further west
towards the desert, where there were vast grassy landscapes, it was clear that the region was
too arid to support trees, but these open landscapes, seasonally home to migrant pastoralists
and their herds, were also easily labelled as “wastelands”. This world view truly missed the
grasses for the absent trees. It failed to recognise that the productivity of these ecosystems lay
in the abundant grazing animals and livestock supported by the grass, and that the livestock
products they generated were the heart of a thriving economy based on adaptive and mobile
pastoralism. (science, 486 words)

XVII. Two men who harassed and stalked a Portuguese tourist were arrested last month; a 14-year-
old boy from Goregaon who went missing was traced in Rajasthan weeks ago; the man
who stabbed a Mumbai professor was arrested within two days in January; and, nearly a year
ago, the alleged attacker of actor Saif Ali Khan was nabbed days after the hunt had hit a dead-
end.
All of these successful police investigations were aided by one crucial tool: the Facial
Recognition System (FRS), linked to 463 of the 3,675 CCTV cameras in the Mumbai Division of
the Railway Protection Force (RPF), covering 114 stations from Churchgate to Surat in the
north and up to Jalgaon in the east. According to officials, Western Railway was the first
division in the country’s rail network to install FRS linked to CCTV cameras. “From last year,
they are being installed in other divisions as well — eventually, the entire network will be
covered. We get requests for assistance from police forces across the country and Central
agencies,” a Western Railway official said. Sources said Mumbai Police units, which operate
over 5,000 cameras, are also linking FRS to their network.
The FRS-equipped CCTV cameras are connected to software available at Mumbai Central or
RPF police stations along the division. If a person on the watchlist passes any of these
cameras, the software immediately issues an alert, triggering a chain of actions. In addition to
photographs of accused persons uploaded after incidents, images of suspects are also fed into
the system. www.lawpreptutorial.com
In 2024 alone, over 10,000 photographs of individuals being tracked by agencies such as the
NIA and CBI were uploaded. “So, even if the person may not have been spotted till then, once
the person enters the platform, we get a hit on the system,” the official said. Another key
feature of the system is its ability to map patterns in an individual’s movements, which helps
investigators track suspects. (Technology, 321 words)

XVII. Winters in Rajasthan are becoming warmer and shorter. During the winter season spanning
November-December 2025 and the first three months of 2026, the region received far less
rainfall than is typical for this time of year. Cold wave days have also declined. Under normal
conditions, Rajasthan experiences around five to six active Western Disturbances — weather
systems that bring winter rain and help intensify the cold. This year, however, only two or
three such disturbances were recorded, according to data from the India Meteorological
Department (IMD).
The consequences are already visible. The growing number of warmer days during winter is
affecting daily life as well as agricultural cycles. For sheep-rearers, the seasonal rhythm has
been disrupted. The end of winter is usually when sheep are sheared, but fluctuating
temperatures are creating new risks. Animals that have already been sheared are developing
pneumonia due to cold nights, while those yet to be sheared are falling ill because of unusually
warm days.
Chatar Singh Jam, a farmer and environmentalist from Jaisalmer said, “In western
Rajasthan, winter used to set in between November 10 and 15,” he says. “This year, it arrived
nearly a month late, around December 15 or 16.” According to him, the intense cold lasted
barely 20 to 25 days, ending by mid-January. “The ground turned white, as if someone had
sprinkled salt over it,” he recalls. “The cold scorched Khejri and Ker trees. But immediately
after Sankranti, the cold vanished, and now temperatures are hovering around 40 degrees
Celsius (°C).” He contrasts this with earlier decades. “In the desert, years with low rainfall
used to bring harsher winters, because dry soil loses heat quickly. But even 10 years ago, days
during winter would still feel cool despite sunshine. Now, you begin to feel heat even in winter
afternoons.” He also points to a shift in wind patterns. “Typically, north-westerly winds would
sweep across the desert during this season. This time, those moisture-laden winds did not
arrive. That directly affected crops.” The impact has been severe. Moisture in Khadins, or
traditional water-harvesting structures, evaporated faster than usual. “We call it the crops
‘thirsting’,” he explains. “Germination declined. Farmers delayed sowing, waiting for the right
conditions. Then, when a short spell of intense cold arrived, it scorched mustard and gram
crops.” (climate, 379 words)
